days.text:

days.label: The secretary I didn't pick (Rob's own story, carousel)
days.title: The Best Person I Ever Worked With
days.text:
The best person I ever worked with is someone I didn't get to pick, and didn't want.

She took my secretary job on seniority. She did not like me. I had the whole year figured out before she ever sat down at that desk.

I was wrong about every part of it. Swipe for the rest. 👉

Principals: who's the person at your school you were wrong about? School secretaries: tag the principal who couldn't have done it without you. 👇

I talk about leading people like this in my keynotes and school workshops. Link in bio.

days.title: "You Keep Talking Policy Instead of My Child"
days.text:
A parent says: "You keep talking policy instead of my child." ⚖️

What's your next sentence?
A) Restate the policy
B) Name their concern, then connect the policy to their child
C) Schedule a follow-up
D) Hand it to the family liaison

Pick a letter below. 👇

This is one of the practice moments in Trust Construction, one of the 8 Factors in my free H.E.L.P. course for school leaders. "People trust what they can predict under pressure."

days.title: Digital Citizenship: Home or School?
days.text:
Digital citizenship has become as commonplace as physical citizenship. 🌍📱

I wrote that in The Future Ready Challenge. Our kids live in two worlds at once, and they need to be good citizens in both.

So here's the debate: who should teach it? Home, school, or both? Tell me in the comments 👇

days.label: What would you do? Scenario 10, Just This Once
days.title: Principals: What Would You Do? Just This Once
days.text:
Principals and teachers: what would you do? 🤔

Parents ask for exceptions "just this once." Usually the answer is no.

Then: a student is assigned out-of-school suspension, and the family says plainly it will be a vacation day. Another student misses a major project for a private family reason you know but can't share with the teacher.

Same rule for everyone, or an exception? Comment your call. What I chose is in the first comment.

This is one of 12 real scenarios in my What Would You Do? 12 School Leadership Scenarios deck, where you make the call before you see how I handled it. Link in bio.

#principallife #schoolleadership #assistantprincipal #whatwouldyoudo #teachersofinstagram #teachertok
days.first_comment:
What I chose: I made the exception when I had enough context to know it served the child and the real purpose of the rule. The out-of-school suspension that would have become an unsupervised vacation became in-school suspension, so the consequence still had structure. For the student with the private family reason, I asked the teacher for an extension without sharing the family's confidence. It was never about favors. It was the right tool for the situation.

A fair decision is not always an identical decision.

Practice decisions like this free: https://www.drrobfurman.com/human-equation-suite/leadership-sim?utm_source=social&utm_campaign=wk2026-11-16-fri

days.text:

linkedin.text:
Parents ask for exceptions "just this once." Most of the time the answer is no.

Two that weren't simple:

A student was assigned out-of-school suspension. He'd be home with an older sibling while his parent worked, and the family told us plainly it would be a vacation day.

Another student missed a major project for a private family reason. I knew the reason. I couldn't share it with the teacher.

What I chose: I made the exception when I had enough context to know it served the child and the real purpose of the rule. The suspension became in-school suspension, so the consequence still had structure. For the second student, I asked the teacher for an extension without sharing the family's confidence.

It was never about favors. It was the right tool for the situation.

A fair decision is not always an identical decision.

Where do you draw the line between an exception and favoritism?
